I should spread the generated options into createQuery in Svelte components rather than hand-writing a queryFn, so using fetchQuery with the generated options directly fits this pattern. For the wiring browser test, I'll follow the same configureClient fetch stub approach used in the AnnouncementSheet test, setting up an in-memory Phoenix with a test wrapper that supplies a QueryClient.

I also need to check whether `$app/state`'s `page` is available in browser tests, since the dialog relies on `page.data.session?.principal?.id` -- likely `page.data` resolves to an empty object there, which should be fine. I'll also skim the SvelteKit section of notes.md for relevant rules around runes controllers and browser test conventions.

## SvelteKit (current)

- Type check with `pnpm check` not `tsc` (Svelte compiler required). It also runs `check:sw`, because the service worker (`src/service-worker/index.ts`) is a separate TS project extending `$app/tsconfig/service-worker` and is excluded from the root `tsconfig.json`.
- Imports use `#lib/...` Node subpath imports (`package.json` `imports`), not `$lib`, and must name the file: `#lib/utils.js`, `#lib/components/ui/button/index.js`. `components.json` aliases use `#lib` so shadcn-svelte generates the same.
- Environment variables are declared once in `src/env.ts` (`defineEnvVars`) and imported from `$app/env/public` / `$app/env/private`; `$env/*` is not used. Optional variables use a pass-through schema so they are `undefined` when unset (call sites rely on `??`). SvelteKit reads them from its own `env.dir`, set to `../..` in `vite.config.ts` to match Vite's `envDir` — keep the two in sync.
- Vitest browser tests run `src/vitest-browser-setup.ts`, which defines the `globalThis.__sveltekit_dev` bootstrap that SvelteKit-rendered pages provide; without it any component importing a dynamic `$app/env/public` variable fails to load. Do not replace it with `vi.mock` (the anti-slop lint bans module mocking).
- `redirect(...)` to an external URL needs `{ external: true }` (or an origin allowlist); the Discord OAuth hop in `members/signup/[invitationId]/discord/+server.ts` uses `external: true` because Phoenix owns the provider URL, which differs per environment.
- Server `handleError` receives every error in SvelteKit 3, discriminated by `kind`; `hooks.server.ts` only console-logs `kind: "unknown"`. `error(status, message)` takes the message as a string; extra `App.Error` properties go in a third argument.
- `pnpm-workspace.yaml` allows Kit 3 for `runed`'s optional `@sveltejs/kit` peer until runed widens its range; remove the rule once it does.
- E2E tests need unique data: `test-${Date.now()}-${randomSuffix}@example.com`
- Use `dinero.js` for money, `day.js` for dates
- TanStack Query uses thunk pattern: `createQuery(() => ({...}))`
- Cookies required by SvelteKit remote functions must use `path: "/"`, because remote form requests are sent to `/_app/remote/...` rather than the page route. Delete those cookies with the same root path.
- Stripe sync scheduling is Phoenix/Oban-owned through `Dhc.StripeSync.Worker`; the legacy Supabase `functions/stripe-sync` edge function and its manual E2E spec have been removed.
- Members dashboard status filtering supports three states: `active`, `inactive`, `paused`; `paused` means `is_active = true` and `subscription_paused_until` is in the future.
- `member_management_view` now exposes computed `membership_status` (`active`/`inactive`/`paused`) plus `paused_until` aliasing `member_profiles.subscription_paused_until` for member list filtering.
- Responsive detail sheets (equipment, my-loans, operator loan queue) use `Sheet.Content side="bottom-right"`. Do not compose `side="bottom"` with `sm:slide-in-from-right`: `tailwindcss-animate`'s `animate-in` keyframes use both `--tw-enter-translate-x` and `--tw-enter-translate-y`, so the two utilities together slide diagonally. Tests: `apps/web/src/lib/components/ui/sheet/sheet-motion.test.ts`.
- Inventory **UI copy** says quartermaster / item / gear / code — never operator, physical unit, register, or slug. Backend actors, capabilities, and OpenAPI stay `operator`. Voice table: `design-system/dublin-hema-club/pages/inventory.md`.
- Training Announcement **copy presets** (`apps/web/src/lib/training-announcements/copy.ts`) are frontend constants carrying the retired Discord bot's wording; the stored source omits `@everyone` because Phoenix prepends the mention line from the announcement's mention setting (a typed mention would double up or never ping). The one accepted drift is the thread name: the bot posted `Roll call September 25`, announcements render `Roll call Thursday 25 September`.
- Training Announcement template fields in the announcement and Change text drawers use `ui/template-input.svelte`: placeholders are atomic, noneditable inline tags, while the bound value remains the API's `{{token}}` string. Change text keeps empty fields empty so the command sends `null` to inherit existing copy. The empty contenteditable leaf owns its DOM children exclusively; keep copy/cut/paste at that serialized boundary and use browser tests for caret/deletion behavior. Assert rendered tags with textbox text content, and serialized syntax against API request bodies.
- Training Announcement UI copy uses direct action labels and short explanations: “Manage posts”, “Change text”, and “Delivery details”. Keep timezone rules in technical documentation rather than repeating Europe/Dublin in the UI. Describe posting restrictions in plain language; Discord message presets remain separate from dashboard wording.
- The Training Announcement occurrence inspector shows a preview for posting outcomes, or a single reason for an unsent post. Translate the API outcome (delivery facts take precedence) rather than displaying its internal `chain`/`decidedBy` checklist; an unsent message is not presented as “What members see”.
- Runes modules (`*.svelte.ts` controllers) are tested as `*.svelte.browser.test.ts`. The unit project runs Svelte's server build in Node, where `$state`/`$derived` and TanStack observers don't react, so a unit test of a runes module passes or fails misleadingly. Create the controller inside `$effect.root` and pass a real `QueryClient`; assert on TanStack pending flags with `vi.waitFor`. `mise run test-unit` runs the browser project too.
- To unit-test a TanStack mutation without a component, build its plain options and run `new MutationObserver(queryClient, options).mutate(vars)`; pass side effects (toasts) in as parameters rather than mocking.
- The browser test project loads no Tailwind, so both responsive layouts render at once: tell desktop from mobile by accessible structure (`getByRole("table")` vs a labelled `list`), not by viewport. Wrappers for components using `Tooltip.Root` need a `Tooltip.Provider` (the app gets it from `sidebar-provider.svelte`).
- The `phoenix` JS package ships no types; they are hand-declared in `src/phoenix.d.ts`. A Phoenix `Socket` reconnects with its original `authToken`, and socket tokens live 60 s, so the notification bridge (`notification-realtime.svelte.ts`) owns reconnection with a fresh token instead of Phoenix's loop.
- In agent shells `pnpm` may not be on PATH: use `mise exec -- pnpm …`. Run the Svelte autofixer from `apps/web` with `mise exec -- npx -y @sveltejs/mcp svelte-autofixer <file> --async` (`--async` matches `experimental.async` in `vite.config.ts`).
- When stubbing ky `fetch` in browser tests, `request.clone().json()` **rejects on an empty body** — bodiless POST/DELETE mutations then fail like network errors before the stub records anything. Catch it and record `undefined` (see `AnnouncementsRail.browser.test.ts`).
- `apps/web/src/lib/components/calendar/dhc-calendar.css` is shared by `TrainingCalendar.svelte` and `workshops/workshop-calendar.svelte`, so its phone rules affect both — check both when editing it.
- Throwaway prototypes under `routes/dashboard/prototype/**` still sit in the shared GitButler workspace, so they must pass the anti-slop lint. Look fixture rows up through a throwing `must()` helper or a type guard instead of using unexplained `as` assertions, and validate lookup tables with `satisfies` instead of annotating a widened `Record<…>` binding. Commit them to a `prototype/<ticket>-<name>` branch, not to main. After you edit a prototype's module-level store (`*.svelte.ts` singleton) while `mise run dev` is running, a full page reload can still load two instances of it: components then read different state (a dialog's Save "succeeds" but nothing updates). Restart the Vite dev server before you debug that symptom.
- Svelte's dev runtime warns `assignment_value_stale` for arrow handlers whose concise body returns an assignment to a `$state` object property, e.g. `onclick={() => (store.dialog = …)}`. Use a block body: `() => { store.dialog = …; }`. TypeScript `as const` inside a ternary in markup (`{#each cond ? ([…] as const) : …}`) fails to parse, so hoist the list into the script.
- Month calendars use `height: "auto"` so week rows contain the shared day-cell minimum height. A fixed root height can squeeze rows below that minimum (observed: 99px rows containing 120px cells), exposing two horizontal borders and overlapping subsequent weeks. Training's Week switch uses the `List` plugin's `listWeek` view: announcements are whole-day occurrences, so an hourly time grid is not useful. The theme callback must preserve the active plugin's view classes (`ec-day-grid ec-month-view` / `ec-list ec-week-view`); scope date-circle and cell-minimum styles to the month grid, not list headings.

## Phoenix (in progress)

- **Dev database** prefers `DATABASE_URL`; if absent it falls back to local Supabase Postgres (`localhost:54322`, user `postgres`, password `postgres`, database `postgres`). Use `POSTGRES_*` env vars only when `DATABASE_URL` is not set.
- **Phoenix CORS dev origins** must include both `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` forms (e.g. `https://127.0.0.1:5173`) because the Vite dev server may bind to `127.0.0.1` and browsers treat that as a separate origin from `localhost`.
- **Sentry** is configured in `config/runtime.exs` under the `config_env() == :prod` block. It reads `SENTRY_DSN` env var automatically. If unset, no events are sent.
- **Sentry Logs metadata** is allowlisted in `config :sentry, logs: [metadata: ...]`; adding `Logger.info/2` metadata is not enough for it to appear in Sentry. Add new structured log keys to both baseline `config/config.exs` and prod `config/runtime.exs` when introducing operational metadata.
- **Sentry integrations**: `Sentry.PlugContext` in the endpoint (request context on errors), Oban integration (failed job capture + cron monitoring), `Sentry.LoggerHandler` (forwards `Logger.error/1` and crashes to Sentry).
- **All 11 Ecto baseline migrations** are marked "up" on the shared Supabase Postgres. The tables already existed from Supabase migrations; Ecto migration versions were inserted into `schema_migrations` to mark them as run.
- If `mix test`/`mix ecto.migrate` reports duplicate baseline objects such as `type "role_type" already exists` against local Supabase, the database has Supabase schema objects but missing Ecto `schema_migrations` rows; do not add duplicate migrations to fix this. Restore/mark the baseline migration versions or use the documented shared Supabase Postgres state.
- **First-time Phoenix setup** on a fresh database: `mix setup` (deps.get + ecto.create + ecto.migrate).
- **Workshop Announcements Worker** (`Dhc.WorkshopAnnouncements.Worker`): Migrated from `process-workshop-announcements` Deno edge function. Fan-out pattern: one incoming Oban job produces downstream `Dhc.Discord.Worker` and `Dhc.Email.Worker` jobs. Context module (`Dhc.WorkshopAnnouncements`) handles DB queries and message formatting, keeping the worker focused on job orchestration.
- **Migrated Oban worker data access**: keep workers as orchestration modules. Put Postgres queries behind domain repository modules such as `Dhc.Invitations.Repository` or `Dhc.StripeSync.Repository` so the worker interface stays small and data access has locality. Prefer Ecto schemas/repositories for migrated tables over carrying forward raw SQL from edge functions.
- **Phoenix API auth**: protected JSON endpoints accept only the signed `_dhc_session` cookie through `DhcWeb.Plugs.RequireSession`. Controllers read `current_session.principal` and live `user_roles`; production bearer-token and Supabase JWT compatibility has been removed.
- **Array unnest distribution queries**: to count elements of a Postgres array column in Ecto (e.g. `Dhc.Members.weapon_distribution/0` over `member_profiles.preferred_weapon[]`), use an `inner_lateral` join over a `SELECT col FROM unnest(?) AS t(col)` fragment and address the named column via `w.col` (e.g. `select: %{weapon: w.weapon, value: count()}`). Ecto rejects selecting the *whole* fragment binding (`w`), so the unnested value must be given a real column name via `AS t(weapon)` inside the fragment and referenced as `w.weapon`. The lateral join lets the fragment reference the correlated outer array column.
- **Phoenix dev authentication**: local authentication uses Phoenix Principals, magic links, opaque Sessions, and Discord OAuth. It does not require Supabase Auth URL, anon-key, or service-role credentials.
- **Migrated Supabase timestamp columns**: legacy tables such as `user_profiles` and `invitations` use `created_at`/`updated_at`, not Ecto's default `inserted_at`/`updated_at`; schemas should use `timestamps(inserted_at: :created_at, type: :utc_datetime)` when mapping those tables.

Good, the signal only aborts on the stop path. Now I'm setting up the reactivation machine file, defining the input shape with memberId and startDate, pulling in the payment method, coverage, and fee mode types from the api-client, and wiring the initial start date from the reactivation window's earliest value.

I'm defining the actors for looking up the reactivation preview, performing the reactivation, and opening the billing portal, along with host-provided actions for reporting outcomes, reconciling caches, opening the portal, surfacing portal failures, and closing. For final states I'm using the paymentState vocabulary directly—succeeded, terminal, pending, needsAction—routed through guards on the actor output, with context tracking memberId, the selected start date and fee mode, the payment method, coverage, and any problem message, plus a SELECT event to update the selection.

The SELECT event should keep the previous error until the next confirm rather than clearing it, and CONFIRM should be guarded on having a nonempty start date and chargeable coverage. I'm keeping the view logic separate as a pure `reactivationView(snapshot)` function so the modal just consumes plain view props, and making sure CLOSE during the lookup state cancels the fetch cleanly, with the noSavedMethod header pulling coverage info from the preview context.

Now I'm structuring the view type so coverage sits at the top level alongside a discriminated phase field—lookingUp, lookupFailed, noSavedMethod, ready, or finished—each carrying only the fields relevant to that phase. For the finished phase, I need to think through the brief frame between the final state and the dialog actually unmounting.

I'm checking whether the Dialog unmount is synchronous enough to avoid a visible flash, and comparing that to how members-table currently handles the closing animation. I'm also reconsidering whether the parent container should own the conditional render or whether callers should wrap the dialog with a keyed block based on the target member id, and whether that key is actually necessary when the id changes.

A cleaner option might be to have the dialog itself handle a stale memberId internally, but that would require moving the machine initialization into a nested component so it can react to prop changes. I'm weighing a simpler but riskier approach — reading memberId once with untrack and documenting that it must be keyed by callers — against splitting the component into a wrapper that keys an inner reactivation session component.

I'm settling on the caller-keys approach with documentation: the members table and the detail page both need to wrap the dialog with a key, since SvelteKit reuses the same page component across route param changes, so the memberId could silently go stale otherwise. <script lang="ts">
import {
	createMutation,
	createQuery,
	useQueryClient,
} from "@tanstack/svelte-query";
import {
	membersAnalyticsQueryKey,
	membersListQueryKey,
	membersMeQueryKey,
	membersShowQueryKey,
	membershipBillingPortalMutation,
	membershipReactivateMutation,
	membershipReactivationPreviewAmountsOptions,
	membershipReactivationPreviewOptions,
} from "@dhc/api-client";
import { useMachine } from "@xstate/svelte";
import { fromPromise } from "xstate";
import { page } from "$app/state";
import { untrack } from "svelte";
import { toast } from "svelte-sonner";
import {
	reactivationMachine,
	reactivationView,
	type ReactivationOutcome,
} from "#lib/membership/reactivation-machine.js";
import { reactivationStartWindow } from "#lib/membership/reactivation-start-window.js";
import ReactivateMembershipModal from "./reactivate-membership-modal.svelte";

/**
 * One reactivation dialog for one member (ALE-252, ALE-450). Mount it only
 * while the dialog is open, keyed by the member: it runs its own
 * `reactivationMachine` actor, which stops when this unmounts, so a late
 * answer for a previous member can never reach a replacement.
 *
 * TanStack Query owns every read and the cache: the machine's actors are the
 * generated preview query and mutations, and the amounts preview is a query
 * keyed off the machine's selection.
 */
let {
	memberId,
	/** The dialog finished (an outcome, or dismissed): unmount it. */
	onClose,
	/** Extra caller-side reconciliation (e.g. SvelteKit load dependencies). */
	onSettled,
}: {
	memberId: string;
	onClose: () => void;
	onSettled?: () => Promise<void> | void;
} = $props();

const queryClient = useQueryClient();
// Read once: the machine is this member's, and so is everything below.
const member = untrack(() => memberId);
// One reading for the machine's initial start date and the date picker.
const startWindow = reactivationStartWindow();

const reactivateMutation = createMutation(() => membershipReactivateMutation());
const billingPortalMutation = createMutation(() =>
	membershipBillingPortalMutation(),
);

const OUTCOME_TOASTS: Record<ReactivationOutcome, () => void> = {
	succeeded: () =>
		toast.success("Membership reactivated.", { position: "top-right" }),
	terminal: () =>
		toast.error(
			"Reactivation submitted, but the bank declined the charge. Use the billing portal to sort out payment.",
			{ position: "top-right", duration: 10000 },
		),
	pending: awaitingBank,
	needs_action: awaitingBank,
};

function awaitingBank() {
	toast.info(
		"Awaiting bank confirmation. SEPA direct debits usually settle within a few business days.",
		{ position: "top-right", duration: 10000 },
	);
}

/** Runs after the dialog closed; it outlives this component on purpose. */
async function reconcile(reactivated: string) {
	const ownProfile = page.data.session?.principal?.id === reactivated;
	await Promise.all([
		queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: membersListQueryKey() }),
		queryClient.invalidateQueries({
			queryKey: membersShowQueryKey({ path: { memberId: reactivated } }),
		}),
		queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: membersAnalyticsQueryKey() }),
		ownProfile
			? queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: membersMeQueryKey() })
			: Promise.resolve(),
	]);
	await onSettled?.();
}

const { snapshot, send } = useMachine(
	reactivationMachine.provide({
		actors: {
			lookUpMethod: fromPromise(async ({ input, signal }) => {
				const options = membershipReactivationPreviewOptions({
					path: { memberId: input.memberId },
				});
				// Closing mid-lookup cancels the request the query client runs.
				signal.addEventListener("abort", () => {
					void queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: options.queryKey });
				});
				const response = await queryClient.fetchQuery(options);
				return response.data;
			}),
			reactivate: fromPromise(async ({ input }) => {
				const response = await reactivateMutation.mutateAsync({
					path: { memberId: input.memberId },
					body: input.selection,
				});
				return response.data;
			}),
			openBillingPortal: fromPromise(async ({ input }) => {
				const response = await billingPortalMutation.mutateAsync({
					path: { memberId: input.memberId },
					body: { returnUrl: window.location.href },
				});
				return response.data;
			}),
		},
		actions: {
			report: (_, outcome) => OUTCOME_TOASTS[outcome](),
			reconcile: ({ context }) => {
				void reconcile(context.memberId);
			},
			showPortal: (_, { url }) => {
				window.open(url, "_blank", "noopener,noreferrer");
			},
			portalFailed: (_, { detail }) => {
				toast.error(detail);
			},
			close: () => onClose(),
		},
	}),
	{ input: { memberId: member, startDate: startWindow.earliest.toString() } },
);

const view = $derived(reactivationView($snapshot));
const selection = $derived($snapshot.context.selection);

// Stripe-computed amounts for the chosen selection, fetched only once a
// saved method exists (otherwise the operator gets the billing-portal
// fallback instead). Keyed by startDate AND annualFeeMode, so changing
// either refetches. Failure degrades gracefully: the modal hides amounts and
// keeps the form usable, so this query failing never blocks a valid charge.
const reactivationAmounts = createQuery(() => ({
	...membershipReactivationPreviewAmountsOptions({
		path: { memberId: member },
		query: {
			startDate: selection.startDate,
			annualFeeMode: selection.annualFeeMode,
		},
	}),
	enabled: view.phase === "ready",
}));
</script>

<ReactivateMembershipModal
	{view}
	{selection}
	{startWindow}
	amounts={reactivationAmounts.data?.data ?? null}
	isLoadingAmounts={reactivationAmounts.isFetching}
	onSelect={(next) => send({ type: "SELECT", ...next })}
	onConfirm={() => send({ type: "CONFIRM" })}
	onOpenBillingPortal={() => send({ type: "OPEN_PORTAL" })}
	onClose={() => send({ type: "CLOSE" })}
/>

On the detail page, I'm swapping the boolean modal flag for a `reactivatingMemberId` state that tracks which member is being reactivated, so the dialog opens keyed to that specific member and clears itself on close or settle, triggering a detail invalidation afterward.

Actually there's a subtlety: if navigation happens while the modal is open, the stale captured id would cause invalidation to target the wrong closure value once state resets to null. The cleanest fix is just changing `onSettled` to pass the memberId directly as an argument instead of relying on closure capture, so the detail page can invalidate using that passed value while the table callback simply ignores it.

# E2E TESTING

Playwright end-to-end tests backed by Phoenix and a disposable PostgreSQL database.

## Running

```bash
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_... mise run test-e2e
# or
pnpm --filter @dhc/web test:e2e
```

Playwright owns the full run lifecycle. Do not manually start PostgreSQL, Phoenix, Supabase, or SvelteKit first.

Run focused specs through the documented mise task (`mise run test-e2e --
e2e/example.spec.ts`), not a direct filtered workspace invocation, so the same
task environment and server lifecycle are used as full runs.

The suite uses the real Stripe test API and rejects missing keys and all keys that
do not start with `sk_test_`. Never run it with live-mode credentials. The Stripe
test account must have active membership prices under the lookup keys used by the
application. Every spec that creates customers, subscriptions, coupons, or
promotion codes owns cleanup from the first successful resource creation, except
durable account configuration explicitly shared with the application. The tier
signup spec creates missing `DHC_COACH_TIER` / `DHC_STUDENT_TIER` coupons and
retains them just like membership prices.

- `playwright.config.ts` starts the `e2e-phoenix-server` and `e2e-web-server` mise tasks; their task-local `env` tables define the test server environment.
- `playwright.config.ts` keeps `serviceWorkers: "block"`. The ALE-270 shell-caching worker re-issues same-origin requests from the worker, which bypasses `page.route` mocks (e.g. the Discord acceptance mock) without changing app behavior — every mocked-navigation test fails with the app working fine. Do not remove the block; the PWA shell spec asserts on static output only by design.
- `mix e2e.server` starts the application through a custom Mix task, so E2E-only Stripe coupon overrides are read in `config/test.exs` when `E2E_SERVER=true`; do not rely on production-only runtime configuration for the test server.
- `playwright.config.ts` appends its process ID to the configured `E2E_COMPOSE_PROJECT` prefix. Phoenix and global teardown inherit that value, giving every run an isolated Compose project instead of attaching to a stale database from another worktree.
- `mix e2e.server` starts the root Compose `test-db` through testcontainers-elixir, reads its dynamic port, migrates it, and starts Phoenix on `127.0.0.1:4000`.
- Keep the E2E Oban configuration at `plugins: []`, not `plugins: false`. Oban 2.23 uses peer leadership to stage scheduled jobs; `false` disables leadership even when queues are enabled and leaves delayed recovery jobs unexecuted.
- Global setup calls `POST /api/e2e/reset`, truncating application tables and restoring base settings.
- The suite currently uses one Playwright worker because legacy specs share run-level state. Add worker-partitioned databases before raising `workers`.
- HTML output is written to `apps/web/playwright-report`; machine-readable output is `apps/web/test-results/playwright-results.json`.

Docker and the Playwright Chromium/Firefox binaries are required. Install browsers with `pnpm --filter @dhc/web exec playwright install chromium firefox`.

On a macOS Docker VM (Colima, OrbStack, Lima, or Docker Desktop) the testcontainers harness needs the socket named on both sides, because the client and the container see different filesystems: `DOCKER_HOST` must be the client-side socket (e.g. `unix://$HOME/.colima/default/docker.sock`, since `DOCKER_HOST` is unset and `/var/run/docker.sock` is only a dangling symlink to Docker Desktop), and `TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=/var/run/docker.sock` must be the VM-side path that `mix e2e.server` bind-mounts into the Postgres container. Without them the harness fails before any test runs, with `{:docker_socket_not_found, ...}` and then `error while creating mount source path ... operation not supported`.

## Phoenix test harness

The `/api/e2e/*` routes exist only when Phoenix compiles with `E2E_SERVER=true` under `MIX_ENV=test`. Every request requires the `x-e2e-harness-key` header. Never expose these routes in dev or production.

Use helpers from `setupFunctions.ts` for named domain fixtures:

- `createMember()`
- `setupWaitlistedUser()`
- `setupInvitedUser()`
- `createWorkshop()`

Membership pause/resume tests need an immediately active Stripe subscription:
pass `createSubscription: true` and `subscriptionPaymentMethod: "card"` to
`createMember()`. SEPA fixtures have an asynchronous payment lifecycle. Choose a
resume date at least two days ahead so request time cannot cross the one-day
validation boundary.

Use `seedE2EScenario()`, `updateE2EFixture()`, and `deleteE2EFixture()` for harness-only setup and cleanup. The harness intentionally has no generic query or raw database client; add a named scenario backed by a Phoenix context when a test needs a new fixture shape.

26:| Change the Training Announcements dashboard page (rail, side sheet, preview) | `apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/training-announcements/` (route: `+page.server.ts` requires `training_announcements.manage`, `+page.svelte` chrome) + `apps/web/src/lib/components/training-announcements/` (rail, sheet, card, Discord preview, detail, suppression/override sheets) + `apps/web/src/lib/training-announcements/` (pure schedule/copy/problem/exceptions vocabulary) + capability/nav/route rules in `apps/web/src/lib/server/authorization/` | ALE-330. The route is a thin adapter: `ssr = false`, `require("training_announcements.manage")`, hands the sheet Dublin today. The rail owns the list plus pause/resume/retire/delete mutations and the selected announcement's detail column; the sheet owns create/edit, and its save order is `lib/training-announcements/save-machine.ts` (ALE-448, a per-sheet `useMachine` actor): create is one write; an edit runs `updateSchedule` only when `scheduleChanged` against the authoritative baseline, then `updateCopy` — a copy-only edit must not reschedule or surface warnings, and a schedule refusal never reaches the copy stage. The two edit writes are not atomic: a copy failure after a schedule write rests in `edit.copyFailed` with the schedule kept (no rollback) and retry resumes at the copy stage. The sheet's TanStack mutations stay the injected actors and own the optimistic create row, rollback and list invalidation (`onSettled`, so an abandoned save still reconciles); closing the sheet stops the actor, so a late answer cannot report to or close a replacement sheet. Preview is a plain mutation, not a machine state. ALE-331: the detail column shows the next post by resolved thread name with capped Suppression/Override lists (cap 5 + counts); the two exception sheets own single-date/range creates with field-attached API errors, and removals confirm in place. Kind is fixed after creation. Phoenix decides every refusal; its problem details render against the causing field. Copy presets are frontend constants; the stored source omits `@everyone`. ADR 0026 (Oxlint `no-restricted-imports`) keeps this domain apart from workshops; only the calendar stylesheet is shared. ALE-332: the rail also shows the Month/Week `TrainingCalendar` (pinned height, `window` items as whole-day chips, striped bank-holiday days, read-only holiday items) above the selected detail, each card shows next posts + recent deliveries from `listForAnnouncement`, and the shared `status.ts`/`window.ts` vocabulary owns display statuses, the 400-day horizon and the `datesSet`→`window` translation — calendar chips are single-line with ellipsis so lone posts survive `dayMaxEvents` measurement on phones, and chip content never closes over selection. # Skill: but

# GitButler CLI Skill

Use GitButler CLI (`but`) as the default version-control interface.

## Start Here

Choose the narrowest first command by task; avoid ritual status checks:

```bash
# Selected dirty files/hunks:
but diff

# Commit order, branch/stack placement, conflict overview:
but status

# File IDs, per-commit files, amend details:
but status -fv

# What one applied branch or commit changed, for review:
but diff <branch-or-commit>

# Details for one known branch or commit:
but show <id>
```

Do not run plain `but status` and then `but status -fv` unless the compact output lacks file details needed for the task.

For "commit just/only/specific changes on a new branch", use the fast path:

```bash
but diff
but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>
```

`but commit -b <branch> ...` creates the branch when it does not exist and prints the created commit. Do not run a separate `but branch new`, status command, or verification diff unless the task needs workspace information that the result does not provide.

In a linked worktree, such as `.claude/worktrees/*`, omit `-b` so the commit goes on the branch the worktree has checked out. Use that branch as the new branch; do not stack another one on it. A worktree with a detached HEAD has no branch yet. There, `but commit -b <new-name> -m "<msg>"` creates the branch at HEAD, checks it out in that worktree, and commits to it.

## IDs

The first token on each `but diff` / `but status` line is that line's ID. When a command needs an ID, copy it exactly from the current output; never hardcode or invent one. ID lifetimes differ by entity:

- Changes and sources are **positional, space-separated** IDs (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" uvw:2e4 uvw:e2c`). An uncommitted hunk ID is written `<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (e.g. `uvw:2e4`, copied from bare `but diff`) — the part after the colon is the hunk's ID, **not** a line range (`uvw:16-40` is invalid). Do not invent flags like `--changes` / `--hunk` / `--ids`, pass a line range, or comma-separate IDs — `uvw,qyo` is parsed as one ID and fails.
- `but diff` is the same for files and hunks, committed or not: `but diff <id> <id>` shows each in turn. Bare `but diff` shows all uncommitted files. A commit or branch must be its only target, because it doesn't compare two of them; `git diff <a> <b>` does. `--stat` lists changed files and line counts instead of patches.
- A committed file is `<commit-id>:<file-id>` (e.g. `mzm:uvw`, shown under each commit). A committed hunk is `<commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` and is shown by `but diff <commit-id>`. `@` means the uncommitted area.
- Commit IDs are stable change IDs that survive history edits (`amend`, `squash`, `move`, `uncommit`, `reword`). Commits without a change ID (e.g. upstream-only) lead with a sha prefix instead, and `#N`-suffixed refs disambiguate duplicates — both go stale after history edits, and a stale sha can silently resolve to the wrong commit. The `(sha …)` on verbose commit lines is informational — do not pass it to commands.
- Branch short IDs are snapshot-local selectors. Use full branch names for branch-targeting mutations; short IDs are safe only for immediate read-only inspection.
- File/hunk IDs copied from one diff read generally remain usable across chained commits. If one stops resolving, re-read `but diff` and retry.

**Chaining:** mutation output is concise by default, so you may chain mutations with `&&` off one inspection read. Do not chain branch short IDs through mutations; use full branch names. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details that the mutation result does not provide. Chained `but commit` calls stack in the order written — the first is oldest, each later one goes on top. History edits may run in sequence when every commit ref involved is a change-ID ref; run them one at a time with `--status-after` when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed, or when the next command needs freshly issued IDs. Chaining `but uncommit <id> && but diff` is safe because bare `diff` needs no ID from the uncommit output. Never pipe a mutation through `tail` or `head`: the pipeline then exits with their status, so the next `&&` runs even when the mutation failed.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Use `but` for all write operations. Never run `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git checkout`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `git stash`, or `git cherry-pick`; `but pull --check` fetches. The only exceptions are selecting a side of a conflicted submodule in resolution mode (see Resolve conflicted commits) and creating a missing target branch (see Notes). If the user says a `git` write command, translate it to `but` and run that.
2. Mutation commands print their result without appending workspace status. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs resulting workspace IDs or details; otherwise trust the mutation result and do not run a verification status/diff.
3. Branches marked `(merged upstream)` have landed; start new work on another branch. That marker alone does not mean `but pull` removes them: run `but pull --check` first. `but pull` removes only branches listed `[integrated]` ("has been integrated upstream and removed locally", or "has been merged into <target> and removed" when the target has no upstream) and rebases the rest, which stay applied. To clear a landed branch that stays applied, use `but unapply <branch>` (acts on its whole stack) rather than `but discard`. `push` and mutations (`commit`, `amend`, `squash`, `uncommit`, `reword`, `move`) refuse landed branches and commits, `absorb` skips them with a notice, and `commit` skips them when picking a default target.
4. Keep going between routine `but` commands. Put any status note in the same message as the next command, and don't end a turn on a summary that announces the next `but` step without running it. Finish with a concise summary.
5. Prefer this skill and `but skill reference` over exploratory help calls. Use `<command> --help` when required syntax is missing or a command fails; use top-level help only when you genuinely need to discover an undocumented command.
6. Other agents may share this checkout, so `@` can hold their edits. Commit, amend, and discard only the IDs or paths you changed. Bare `but commit`, `but absorb`, `but discard @`, and `git stash` take their work too, and a refusal naming files you didn't edit means you selected theirs.

## Command Patterns

- Initialize a Git repository: `but init` (current directory) or `but -C <path> init`. Non-interactive; creates no commits, remotes, or GitButler workspace. Existing repositories are left unchanged. In a repository with no commits, make the first commit with a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"`; `-b` is refused there.

- Commit: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>` — `-b <branch>` creates the branch if it does not exist
- Commit everything uncommitted: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>"` (omit the IDs)
- Several commits from one diff: chain `but commit` calls with `&&` (commits stack oldest-first)
- Never pass `-s` to `commit`, `move`, or `pick`: it is `--switch`, not git's `--signoff`, and it unapplies every other stack.
- The branch is never positional (`but commit <branch>` fails; use `-b`), and `but amend` needs `-t` when several branches are applied.
- Commit at a specific history position: `--above <commit-or-branch>` or `--below <commit-or-branch>` (mutually exclusive). With a branch target, add `-b <new-name>` to name the new branch; otherwise its name is generated. The name must not already exist. Do not combine `-b` (even without a name) with commit/worktree targets.
- Targeting is **required** when more than one **stack** is applied; without it `but commit` fails with "Unclear where to commit. Found more than one stack". Several branches stacked together count as one stack — an untargeted commit then silently lands on the stack's top branch, so pass `-b` whenever the branch matters.
- Always pass `-m "<msg>"` (or `-F -` with a heredoc, `-F <file>` with a file outside the repository, or `--no-message`) to `but commit`, and to `but squash` whenever its sources are commits or branches unless the target is `@` (squash also takes `-u` to keep the target's message) — those compose a new message; without a flag an agent run keeps whatever the command composed (empty for `but commit`, the joined source messages for `but squash`) and a terminal opens an editor. Squash sources that are uncommitted or committed changes reuse the target's message and need no flag; squashing into `@` rejects message flags outright.
- Amend: `but amend -t <commit-or-branch> <file-or-hunk-id> <file-or-hunk-id>` — a branch target resolves to its newest commit; a branch with no commits takes `but commit` instead. Without `-t` the changes go to the newest commit of the branch checked out where they are, also in a linked worktree; with `gitbutler/workspace` checked out that takes exactly one applied branch
- Uncommit: `but uncommit <commit-id>` (whole commit), `but uncommit <branch>` (all commits and remove branch), `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>` (committed file), or `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (committed hunk); committed files and hunks may be mixed, but all must come from one commit
- Copy commits (sources stay unchanged): `but pick <sha> [<sha>...] -b <new-branch>` puts the copies on a new independent branch from the target, `-b <existing-branch>` on that applied branch's tip, and `--above <branch> -b <new-name>` (or `--below`) on a new branch stacked there. Pick applies sources in the order given, so pass them oldest first. For a branch that is not applied, list SHAs with `git log --reverse <target>..<branch>` and inspect them with `git show` or `but show <sha>`; `but diff` and the IDs that `but branch show` prints for it do not work.
- Move committed changes into an existing commit or `@`: `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed file; `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed hunk; all sources must come from one commit
- Move committed changes into a new commit at a chosen position: `but move <commit-id>:<file-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed file; `but move <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed hunk (`--below`, `--branch`, and `--unstack` also work)
- `but split` and a `but move` of committed changes name their new commit with `-m` or `-F` too; without either the commit gets an empty message. `but move` rejects `-m`/`-F` for whole-commit and branch sources.
- Change a commit's message: `but reword <commit-id> -m "<msg>"`, or for a long message `-F -` with a heredoc or `-F <file>` with a file outside the repository; an empty `-F` input is refused. `but reword <branch> -m <new-name>` renames a branch. Without `-m` or `-F` an agent run fails and a terminal opens an editor.
- Move commit to branch top: `but move <commit-id> -b <branch>`
- Move commits or committed changes onto a new named branch: `but move <source> --above <branch> -b <new-name>` (`--below` also works); use `but move <source> --unstack -b <new-name>` for an independent branch. Omit `-b` for a generated name. Naming is not supported when stacking or unstacking a branch source.
- Discard: `but discard <id> [<id>...]` — accepts branches, commits, committed changes, uncommitted changes, or `@` for all uncommitted changes
- Push: `but push <top-branch>` — pushes the selected branch and its ancestors; to update a stack, select its top branch once and never loop. Bare `but push` pushes all unpushed work when run non-interactively — one push per stack (its topmost unpushed branch, ancestors included), and the output lists every branch it pushed. It exits non-zero if any stack failed; stacks that already pushed stay pushed, and rerunning after fixing the failure is safe (up-to-date stacks are skipped). `but push` and `but pr new` replace the remote branch: if others may have pushed to it, bring their commits in first (see Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote).
- Create PR: `but pr new <branch-name> [-m "Title..."] [-F - | -F <file>] [-t] [--draft]` — auto-pushes first; do not run `but push` before it

## Task Recipes

### Update workspace from main

For "get latest from main", "update/sync this workspace", "rebase onto main", or "pull main":

1. `but pull` — one command; no preflight needed. Its output reports the resulting state, and `but undo` reverts it. Uncommitted changes that conflict with the update get conflict markers and show as `{conflicted}`; resolve them as in Conflicts in uncommitted files.
2. If commits come back conflicted, resolve them with the `but resolve conflicts <branch>` and `but resolve apply` loop in Resolve conflicted commits, one branch at a time. When `HEAD` is `gitbutler/workspace`, `but pull` prints `but resolve <commit>` as the next step; that is edit mode, which is only for running code against a resolution.

`but pull --check` answers "would this conflict?" without updating. Do not use it as a routine
preflight; use it when the user asks for a preview, you need a fetch, repository policy requires one, other agents'
branches may move, or an applied branch was just merged upstream (see rule 3).

Rebasing applied branches onto the latest target IS `but pull` — never `move`, `config target`, `unapply`, or raw `git pull`/`git rebase`. The base shown in status is the last FETCHED state: when `git log` shows the remote target (for example `origin/main`) ahead of it, that is exactly the update `but pull` fetches and applies — the target setting is not stale and repointing it is never the fix. Pull carries uncommitted changes along; there is no stash, so do not hand-revert files.

### Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote

`but pull` only rebases onto the target. Commits someone pushed to your branch's remote show in `but status` under `(upstream: on <remote>/<branch>)`, above the branch's own commits; if status may be stale, run `but pull --check` to fetch.

1. `but branch update <branch>`, once, on the branch they pushed to.
2. Then `but pull` if the target moved too. Update before pulling. If the branch was rebased since its last push (for example by an earlier `but pull`), the update leaves an empty `(no changes)` copy of a shared commit. On a single branch, `but discard` that copy by its `#N` ref. In a stack, `but undo` the update and tell the user, because the update can also move commits into the lower branch. Do not update a second time, even if `(upstream: …)` still lists commits, because a second update duplicates commits.

### Commit selected files or hunks

1. `but diff` — shows file and hunk IDs for uncommitted changes. Do not run plain `but status` first.
2. Use file IDs when whole files belong in the commit; use hunk IDs (`<file-id>:<hunk-id>`) when only part of a file belongs. Omit IDs you don't want committed. For whole files or directories, paths work too, from the repo root or the current directory (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" src/ui README.md`; no globs), so don't build ID lists by piping `but diff` through grep.
3. `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id1> <id2>` — the branch is created if it does not exist, so no prior `but branch new` is needed.
4. When the task requires knowing which changes remain, add `--status-after`; otherwise the created-commit result is sufficient.

Edge case: if wanted and unwanted edits are in the same diff hunk, GitButler cannot split that hunk by ID. Only when the task requires keeping part of that hunk uncommitted, temporarily edit the working tree to isolate the wanted lines, commit those IDs, then restore the leftover lines so they remain uncommitted.

### Amend into existing commit

1. `but status -fv` for the target commit ID and file IDs; `but diff` for hunk IDs when only part of a file belongs.
2. `but amend -t <commit-id> <id> <id>` — one command per target commit. For several target commits, chain the amends with `&&` when every target is a change-ID ref; otherwise run them one at a time with `--status-after` to get fresh refs.

### Split an existing commit

For a two-way split, move selected committed files or hunks directly into a new commit:

1. `but diff <source-commit-id>` — read committed file and hunk IDs.
2. `but split <committed-file-or-hunk-id> [<committed-file-or-hunk-id>...] -m "<message>"` — sources may mix files and hunks, but must come from one commit. The command creates the named commit immediately above the source and leaves unselected changes and the original message in the source. No follow-up reword is needed for the new commit.
3. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details not provided by the mutation result.

For more than two replacement commits, repeat `but split ... -m "<message>"` using the remaining source's committed changes, or use the uncommit/recommit workflow below when rebuilding the entire commit:

1. `but status -fv` when you need the source commit, branch name, or placement anchor.
2. `but uncommit <source-commit-id> && but diff` in one shell call exposes the commit's changes and prints the resulting file and hunk IDs. If `but uncommit` refuses because later commits depend on the source, its hint names them, and following it uncommits those commits too. To keep them committed, repeat `but split` instead.
3. Pick replacement contents from that dirty diff, not from the old committed diff.
4. Determine the requested chronological order from the user's wording, then create the replacement commits oldest-first by chaining `but commit` calls. Do not reverse that order to match `but status`, which displays commits newest-first. `-b <branch>` puts each new commit at the TOP of that branch — if the split commit had commits above it, the replacements now sit above those preserved commits.
5. **If commits from that branch must stay ABOVE the replacements, put the preserved block back on top instead of fighting anchors.** Do not anchor with `--above <top>`/`--below <top>` (sha/`#N` anchors go stale as each insert rewrites history). Move the block together so its internal order stays intact: append `&& but move <preserved-id> [<preserved-id>...] -b <branch>` to the commit chain. Change-ID refs from step 1 stay valid; wait for fresh output first if any preserved ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
6. Leave unwanted changes uncommitted. Replacements created oldest-first appear newest-first in status — that is correct; do not reorder them. Add `--status-after` to the final mutation when you need to inspect the resulting order.

### Reorder commits

`but status` displays commits newest/top first, while task specs often list history oldest to newest — translate before moving.

1. `but status` once to get commit IDs (use `-fv` only if you also need file details).
2. `but move <source> --below <target-commit>` places source immediately below target in `but status` (older in oldest-to-newest history). `--above` places it immediately above (newer). `but move <source> -b <branch>` moves it to branch top/newest.
3. For an adjacent block, run ONE move, anchored either way: `but move <block-id> <block-id> --below <following-commit-id>` or `but move <block-id> <block-id> --above <preceding-commit-id>`. Pick an anchor outside the block; source order does not matter and the block keeps its internal order. Add `--status-after` when you need to inspect the resulting order; do not move the anchor or block members again.
4. For other reorders, make the smallest set of moves.

### Squash commits

1. `but status` for commit IDs and order.
2. Name the sources positionally and the result/target commit with `-t`: `but squash <source> [<source>...] -t <target> -m "<new message>"`.
3. To collapse an entire branch into one commit, pass just the branch and no `-t`: `but squash <branch> -m "<new message>"`.
4. Multiple independent groups may run in sequence off one status read (targets keep their change-ID refs); prefer newer/top groups first. Take fresh refs only when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
5. Add `--status-after` to the final squash when you need to inspect the resulting history; do not re-verify with a separate status.

### Stack existing branches

To make one existing branch depend on another: `but move <child-branch-name> --above <parent-branch-name>` (use full branch names; commit reordering uses commit IDs). To unstack: `but move <branch-name> --unstack`.

**DO NOT** stack via `uncommit` + `branch delete` + `branch new --above`, and do not use `but undo` to unstack.

### Work in a linked worktree

1. `but worktree new <branch-name>` checks out that branch in a new directory, creating it if needed (an existing branch must not be in the workspace), and prints that directory. Add `-A <branch-or-commit>` to start the branch there instead of the workspace base; it takes any Git revision, like a SHA or `origin/main`. Worktrees made by other tools must sit outside the repository directory or be listed in `.git/info/exclude`; otherwise a bare `but commit` in the main checkout records them in the branch.
2. Run `but` from that directory, or with `but -C <path>`. There, a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"` or `but diff` takes that worktree's changes, a bare path names a file there, and the commit goes on the worktree's branch. Do the work on that branch, also in a worktree another tool made. `-b <new-name>` is refused there, except in a worktree with a detached HEAD, where it names the worktree's branch; stack a new branch on it only when the user asks for a separate branch. `but undo` doesn't restore a branch a worktree has checked out: after a command that changed that branch, it refuses and changes nothing. Reverse such a command with its inverse (`uncommit`, `reword`, or `move` the commit back), also when you ran it from another checkout. After `but pull`, `but undo` reverts the rest and leaves that branch rebased.
3. `but status` from any checkout shows the worktree as a lane of its own, with the same IDs everywhere. `@` always means the main worktree's uncommitted changes; `<worktree>:@` names a linked worktree's changes from anywhere.
4. Push and open PRs as for any branch (`but pr new <branch-name>`). `but pull` also rebases worktree branches. If that leaves a worktree commit `{conflicted}`, use the `but resolve conflicts <branch>` and `but resolve apply` loop in Resolve conflicted commits; `but resolve <commit-id>` can't check it out.
5. When done, `but worktree remove <name>` deletes the directory and keeps the branch. It refuses while the worktree has uncommitted changes; `-f` discards them. To delete the branch as well, run `but branch delete <name>` afterwards.

### Create or manage pull requests

`but pr new <branch-name>` pushes the selected branch and its ancestors, then creates the PR in one step — no prior `but push`. Provide `-F -` with a heredoc or `-F <file>` (first line is the title), `-t`, or `-m` with real newlines (zsh/bash: `-m $'Title\n\nBody'`) so no editor opens. Do not write the message to a file inside the repository: the next `but commit` would commit it. Changes that build on another branch's commits cannot land on an independent branch. `but commit` and `but amend` fail atomically ("Cannot commit: N changes could not be applied"), naming the branch and commit each rejected change depends on — nothing is committed and no `-b` branch is created.

A refusal can also mean your hunk only borders lines that branch changed (a doc line, a lockfile): then leave one unchanged line between your edit and theirs, or keep that hunk uncommitted until that branch lands, and commit the rest. Never drop or rewrite real work to get past a refusal; ask the user.

When there is a single dependency branch, the error's Hint gives the exact recovery command: `but move <your-branch> --above <dependency-branch>` to stack an existing branch on its dependency, or `but branch new <name> --above <dependency-branch>` when the target branch didn't exist yet. Run it, then retry the original command. When the error names dependencies without a Hint (several dependency branches, or the dependency is on the target branch itself), run `but status -fv` to see where the dependent commits live before choosing a placement.

If that recovery command fails, do NOT try `uncommit`, `squash`, or `undo` as a workaround — re-run `but status -fv` to confirm both branches exist and are applied, then retry with exact branch names.

Find them from the warning that history-editing commands (`move`, `discard`, …) print, from the `but pull` summary, or from `but status`. 1. `but resolve conflicts <branch>` — shows the conflicts of that branch's oldest conflicted commit, numbered per file. Each conflict has three sections: `ours` (the new base the commit was rebased onto), `base` (common ancestor), and `theirs` (the commit's own version). 2. Apply one resolution per command:
   - Merged/mixed content (the common case — combine the intent of both sides): pipe it to `but resolve apply <path>:<N>` via stdin (heredoc) or pass `--file <f>`. The content replaces the whole conflicted region; never include conflict markers.
   - Take a side entirely: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ours` or `--theirs` (bare `<path>` applies the side to all conflicts in that file).
   - Delegate one conflict to the configured AI model: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ai` — prefer your own merged content when you have the context.
   - `apply` targets the same default commit as `conflicts`; when more than one branch is conflicted, pin it with `--commit <branch>`.
3. Go back to step 1 until it reports no conflicts. Commit ids are not stable here — every apply rewrites the commit — but branch names are, so address everything by branch and never bookkeep commit ids. Partial progress is fine: a commit with unresolved conflicts left stays `{conflicted}` with exactly those conflicts.

A wrong resolution is reverted with `but undo`.

`but resolve <commit-id> --ai` resolves a whole commit with the configured AI model in one shot, and `but resolve --ai` without a commit resolves every conflicted commit, oldest first — acceptable as a fallback, but you usually have better context than that model does, so prefer resolving the conflicts yourself with `apply`.

**Use edit mode only when you must run code against the resolution** (build/tests at that commit). Edit mode needs `gitbutler/workspace`: while a single branch is checked out, `but resolve <commit-id>` refuses, so use `apply`.

1. `but resolve <commit-id>` — enters resolution mode and prints the conflict regions.
2. **Edit the files** to remove every conflict marker — `<<<<<<<`, `|||||||` (the common-ancestor section), `=======` and `>>>>>>>` — and keep the correct content. Do NOT skip this; do NOT use `but amend` on conflicted commits.
   - A conflicted submodule has no markers and `finish` refuses until you select its side: see Conflict Resolution Mode in `but skill concepts`.
3. `but resolve finish` reports leftover markers, surviving uncommitted changes, every remaining conflicted commit, and the exact current `but resolve <id>` command. Add `--status-after` to the finish you expect to clear the last conflict only when the task needs the complete resulting workspace. When it says no conflicted commits remain, stop; do not run a verification status. Cancel instead with `but resolve cancel --force`, which drops your resolution edits; without `--force` it refuses once the conflict markers are checked out.
4. Repeat for remaining conflicted commits, oldest first — finishing a lower commit rebases the ones above it.

### Conflicts in uncommitted files

`but status` marks uncommitted files with unresolved merge conflicts `{conflicted}`; they are excluded from committable changes and outside `but resolve` mode. Edit the file to the wanted contents with no conflict markers left (or delete it), then `but resolve <path>...` to mark it resolved with that state; it then shows as an ordinary uncommitted change.

## Git-to-But Map

| git | but |

| `git status` | `but status` for branch/stack/commit overview; `but status -fv` for file details; `but diff` for selected dirty changes |
| `git add` + `git commit` | `but commit -b <branch> -m ... <ids>` |

- `but` needs no setup in a Git repository. `HEAD` is either one checked-out branch, marked `[HEAD]` in `but status`, or `gitbutler/workspace`, which merges every applied stack.
